activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wet mittens and boots are left out to dry after playing in the snow.
story:
Chloe woke up early. Snow was on the ground! "A snow day!" she cheered. She pulled on her boots. She put on her mittens. Out she ran into the backyard.

The snow was cold and soft. Chloe made a big snowball. She patted it with her red mittens. Snow fell from the sky and tickled her nose. She laughed and laughed.

Then Mom called, "Time for a snack!" Chloe ran inside. She wanted hot cocoa. Mom made it, and Chloe watched from her chair.

Soon Chloe wanted to go back out. She grabbed her mittens. But they were wet! Water dripped from them. Her boots were wet too. "Oh no," said Chloe.

"Hang them up to dry," said Mom. Chloe clipped her mittens to the rack. She set her boots by the door. They dripped, drip, drip.

Chloe waited by the window. She watched the snow. At last her mittens felt dry. Her boots felt dry too. On they went! Chloe ran outside fast. She picked up her snowball. "Still here!" she said, and gave it a big pat.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Avery sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. "Mama, we went to the park tomorrow!" she said. Mama smiled and shook her head. "The park was yesterday," Mama said. "Yesterday is the day before today." Avery tapped her ear. Did she hear that right? "Yesterday?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "It already happened."

The car went past the bakery. Avery saw a thin bird on a fence. "Look, a bird!" she said. "It is there now," said Mama. "Now means right this minute." The bird flew away. "Where did it go?" Avery asked. "It will come back later," said Mama. "Later means not now, after now."

"Can we go to the park again?" Avery asked. "We can go tomorrow," said Mama. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Avery clapped her hands. The car turned onto their street. Tomorrow felt far away. But now the car was stopping. Now they were home. Avery jumped down from her seat. "Tomorrow, park!" she called. "Park tomorrow!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Nova went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she stayed home. Today the sun was out. Nova wanted the ice cream truck.

"Is the truck here now?" she asked Mom.

"Not now," said Mom. "The truck comes later."

Nova waited. She went down the slide. She played in the sand. A funny pigeon walked by her bag and pecked at the strap.

"When is later?" Nova asked.

Mom held up her watch. "This clock shows what time it is," said Mom. "See the hands move. When they get to the three, it is later."

Nova watched the clock. The hands moved slow, slow, slow. She kissed the watch face. Then she heard a bell.

The ice cream truck came around the corner.

"Later is now!" said Nova.

"Today it is," said Mom, laughing. "And tomorrow we can come back."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Used needles go into a special hard box so nobody gets poked.
story:
Elias sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse came in with a small tray. "What is that?" Elias asked. "It is your shot," said Dad. The nurse cleaned his arm with a cold wipe. Then came a quick pinch. Elias blinked. It was done!

Then Elias saw a red box on the wall. It was small and hard. "What is that red box for?" he asked. The nurse held up the used needle. "This goes in here," she said. She dropped the needle through the little slot. Clunk. It stayed inside. "So nobody gets poked," she said.

"The needle goes in and the box keeps it?" asked Elias. "Yes," said Dad. "The needle goes in and the box keeps it." Elias watched the slot close. The needle could not come back out. It was safe in there.

Afterward, Dad took Elias to the ice cream shop. Elias got a small pink cone. He took a big lick. "My shot is all done," he said, "and the needle is in the box." Dad smiled and gave him a thumbs up.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries.
story:
Raphael was at Grandma's house. Today was painting day! Grandma set out big paper and bright paints.

"I will paint a sun," said Raphael. He made a big yellow circle. He added orange rays all around. "It looks so sunny!" He wanted to touch it. He poked the sun with one finger.

"Oh no!" The yellow smeared. The sun had a smudge on it now. "My sun!" said Raphael. "It got all blurry."

"Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries," said Grandma. "Let's wait and watch."

Raphael sat very still. He watched his painting. He touched the squishy paintbrush instead. He did not touch the paper. Dad came in with a snack. They ate apple slices together.

Then Grandma said, "Touch it now. Very gently."

Raphael tapped the sun. It felt dry and smooth. Nothing smeared! The sun stayed bright and round.

"It worked!" said Raphael. "I waited and it dried!"

"Thank you for waiting," said Grandma. She hung the painting on the fridge.

Raphael grinned at his sunny picture, then ran to get more paper.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Fans often wear their team's colors to show which team they cheer for.
story:
Anthony ran into the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. A big game was starting soon!

Anthony sat with Mama, Papa, and Aunt Jo. Everyone wore green shirts. Anthony looked down. His shirt was plain and gray.

"I want a green shirt too!" said Anthony.

Aunt Jo opened her big bag. She pulled out a small green shirt. Anthony pulled it on over his gray one. Now he matched everyone!

The game began. The crowd on the screen made a big noise. Lots of fans wore green, just like Anthony's family.

A man at the next table wore green too. He waved at Anthony. Anthony waved back.

"Smart shirt," said Papa with a big smile.

The team ran fast. Anthony jumped up. He clapped and clapped. The green fans on the screen clapped too.

Aunt Jo held up her cup. "Go, green team!" she called.

Anthony held up his little cup of water. "Go, green team!" he shouted.

The room went quiet. Then the screen showed a green player run, run, run. He sent the ball far across the field.

Everyone jumped up. The whole restaurant made one big noise.

Anthony hugged Papa's leg. His green shirt was bright in the light of the big screen.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: The odd one out is the thing that does not belong in a group.
story:
Willow sat on the rug at school. Miss Penny put out a big red box. "Let's sort our things," said Miss Penny. Willow wanted to help put everything away. But the box was all mixed up.

First Willow pulled out toy cars. She put the cars in one pile. All the cars had wheels. Then she pulled out a banana. A banana in the toy pile! "That is the odd one out," said her friend Ben. "It does not belong with the toys." Willow put the banana in the food pile, with apples and bread.

Next Willow found a soft toy bear. She put it in the animal pile, with a cat and a dog. "We learn to sort by looking," said Miss Penny. Now every pile had the same kind of thing. Willow clapped her hands and smiled at her neat piles.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
story:
Sofia wanted to make her own breakfast. Mom said, "You can help." The toast was warm from the toaster. Mom had put it on the plate.

Sofia picked up the butter knife. She took a little butter. She spread it slow and soft. The butter melted and made the toast shiny. "It looks real yellow now," she said. Mom smiled. "You pay attention so well," said Mom.

Next came the milk. Sofia held the big cup with two hands. She poured and poured. The milk went up to the very top. She walked to the table. Step, step, wobble. Milk spilled over the edge. It ran down the cup and onto her hand.

"Hmm," said Sofia. "The cup was too full." She tried again. This time she stopped pouring before the cup was full to the top. She left a little room. She walked to the table. Step, step, wobble. This time nothing spilled at all. Sofia took a big sip. "I did it, Mom!" she said. Mom clapped her hands.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow melts into water when it is brought inside where it is warm.
story:
Anthony looked out the window. Snow was everywhere. No school today! "Snow day!" he shouted. He jumped on the rug. "One sock, two socks, boots, coat, hat!" said Mom. Anthony counted each thing as he put it on. Then he ran outside.

Outside, the sky was dark and gray. Anthony made one big snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it forever. He carried it inside. He set it in his red bowl. "Stay right there," he told the snowball. Then he went to build a rainbow tower of blocks.

The tower got very tall. One block, two blocks, three blocks, four. Boom! It fell over. Anthony laughed. Then he remembered his snowball. He ran to the bowl. The bowl was full of water. No snowball at all. Just a wet puddle. "My snowball ran away!" he cried.

Mom came over. "Look," she said. "The snow came inside where it is warm." Anthony dipped his finger in the water. It was cold water, and that was all. He grinned. He got a spoon and scooped a fresh scoop of snow. "I will watch you this time," he told it. He sat down. One minute, two minutes, three. The snow got small, then smaller. Drip, drip, drip. "Got you!" said Anthony, and he patted the puddle with his spoon.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: In a drawing app, moving your finger across the screen draws a line.
story:
Myles went to Dad's office. He saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I use it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "First you press this little button."

Myles pressed the button. The screen lit up. It went from dark to bright! Dad tapped a green square. "This is the drawing app," he said.

Myles took the tablet. His finger slid across the screen. A red line followed his finger! He moved his finger again. The line went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle. "I made a line," said Myles. The line looked like a squiggle. Myles gave it two eyes. "Now it's a snake," he said. Dad looked up from his work. "A red snake on a green grass day," he said.

Outside, a truck rumbled down the street. Myles drew a long line under the snake. "The snake has a road now," he said.

Soon Myles was tired of drawing. "All done," he said. Dad helped him press the button again. The screen went dark. Myles put the tablet in the drawer, all by himself. "Good job," said Dad. Myles smiled and folded his hands on the desk. "Snakes need naps too," he said.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: Wrapping paper hides a present, so nobody can see what is inside until it is opened.
story:
Liam was three today. His party was at the park. There was cake and balloons. Grandma brought a big box. The box was all wrapped up in paper.

"Is it a truck?" Liam asked. He shook the box. He could not see inside. The paper hid the present. He squeezed it. He held it up to his ear. "Maybe it is a drum," said his cousin Mia. "Maybe it is a duck," said Grandpa. Everyone laughed.

Liam wanted to know now. He picked at the paper with his little fingers. "Not yet," said Mom. "We sing first." So Liam waited. It was hard to wait. He tapped his toes.

Then they sang happy birthday. Liam blew out his candles with Mom right beside him. Then Mom said, "Now you can open it." Liam tore the paper off. Inside was a big red truck! He could not see it before, but now he could. "My truck!" Liam shouted. He pushed it down the hill. "Beep beep," said Grandpa. "Coming through!" said Liam.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: If you hold a book upside down, the words and pictures look upside down too.
story:
Matteo wanted to read his puppy book all by himself. He sat on the rug and held the book. He looked at the pages. "That looks funny," he said. The puppy's legs were up in the air. The little words were upside down too.

Matteo frowned. "Big problem," he said. He turned his head to one side. The puppy still looked upside down. He turned his head the other way. Still upside down. Matteo laughed a big laugh.

Mama came over and sat close. "You made the pictures pop upside down," she said with a smile. Matteo turned the book around in his hands. Now the puppy stood on his four paws. The little words stood up straight too. "There he is!" said Matteo. He opened the front cover. He turned page after page, one at a time, all the way to the back.

"Read it to me," said Mama. Matteo pointed at the words. "Puppy runs fast," he said. Mama nodded and clapped. Matteo hugged the fresh, smooth pages. Then he flipped the book upside down one more time. The puppy hung by his ears. "Silly puppy," said Matteo. He turned the book right side up again. "Good night, puppy."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In basketball, players score by throwing the ball through a hoop.
story:
Rose sat high in the big stadium. Her dad sat next to her. Her friend Mia sat on the other side. Down below, the players ran fast. Rose watched the ball go up and down the court.

A player threw the ball. It went right through the hoop. The crowd made a big noise like a storm. "Look, the ball went in the hoop!" said Mia. Rose clapped and clapped. Then the players threw the ball through the hoop again and again. Every time it went through, the crowd cheered.

After the game, Dad took Rose to a small hoop. He handed her a ball. Rose planted her feet on the ground. She aimed at the hoop. She threw the ball. It went up, then down, then right through the net. "I did it!" Rose said. Mia laughed and jumped. Rose picked up her spotted ball and lined up for one more throw.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: You can make a new friend by telling someone your name and asking theirs.
story:
Max climbed the steps of the school bus. It was his first day of school. He sat by the window. He held his little bag. He wanted a friend, but he did not have one yet.

A boy sat down next to him. The boy looked at the floor. He did not say anything. Max took a big breath. Then he said, "My name is Max. What is your name?" The boy looked up. He smiled. "I am Sam," he said.

Now Max had a friend. Sam showed Max his sweet red apple from his lunch box. They looked out the window together. A big dog ran by, and both boys laughed. At school, the teacher said, "Sam, you can sit next to Max." Sam sat down and whispered, "This bus is fun." Max nodded and waved out the window at the dog.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A child's age is said with a number word, like 'I am four.'
story:
Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted red apples. Dad said, "We need one, two, three, four, five apples." Sienna put apples in the bag. One, two, three, four, five. The bag felt heavy.

A man at the store smiled at her. "How old are you?" he asked. Sienna held up three fingers. Then she said, "I am three!" The man clapped. "Three is a good age," he said.

At the bread shelf, Sienna counted buns. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Then more. "Seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten buns in a row. Sienna tapped each bun softly as she said the numbers. Dad waited. He let her take her time.

A song played over the speakers. Sienna began to dance. She twirled near the cart. Her shoe landed in a messy puddle by the fruit. Dad laughed. "One wet shoe," he said. He wiped it with a paper towel. "Now let's count our apples again," said Dad. Sienna opened the bag. "One, two, three, four, five!" she said.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Snow melts into water when you bring it inside where it is warm.
story:
Snow was falling outside. Logan pressed his nose to the window. "Snowy!" he shouted. Mom helped him put on his big puffy coat. She zipped his red boots. On went his warm hat.

Outside, the wind whooshed. "Windy!" said Logan. The snowflakes tickled his cheeks. His dog, Bingo, ran in circles. Bingo dug in the snow and found his old bone. "Good boy!" said Logan.

Logan scooped up a snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it forever. He carried it inside. He set it in a cup on the table. "I will keep you," he told the snowball. Then he ran back out to play more.

Later, Mom called, "Snack time!" Logan ran to see his snowball. He looked in the cup. The cup was empty! There was only a little puddle of water. "Where did it go?" he asked. He touched the water. It was wet and cool. His snowy ball had melted in the warm house. Logan clapped his hands. "It turned into water!" he said. Bingo came and licked the puddle. Logan yawned a big, sleepy yawn. "Night night, snowball," he whispered. Mom carried him off to his cozy bed.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
story:
Gabriel ran to the playground. He wanted the big slide, not the small one. The gate to the water park was shut. Gabriel pulled and pulled. It would not open. "Mama, help!" he called.

Mama came fast. Gabriel had tried slow. Mama pushed the gate. Click! It swung wide open. "Look," said Mama. "Open and closed are opposites." Gabriel laughed. He pushed the gate shut. Then he pulled it open. Shut, open, shut, open. What fun!

The water sprinklers were on. Splash, splash! The water felt cold. The sun felt hot. Mama held out a towel. Gabriel dried off, all warm. Then it was quiet. Only the little birds sang. Gabriel waved at the gate. "Bye, gate!" he said. He closed it all by himself.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days.
story:
Juliette was on the swim team. Every day she went to the tall pool with her mommy. She practiced kicking in the water. Her teacher was called Coach Ben.

One day the sun was very hot. Juliette felt slow and hot. The team took a break. All the other kids drank from their bottles. Juliette looked in her bag. Her water bottle was not there. She had left it at home.

"I forgot my bottle," she said. Coach Ben brought over a big water bottle. "Players drink water during breaks," he said. "Especially on hot days." Juliette drank and drank. Soon she felt better. She got back in the pool and kicked fast.

After practice, Mommy helped Juliette pack her bag. The water bottle went in first, every single day. At dinner that night, Juliette told Daddy all about the hot pool. "I will always stay with my water bottle," she said, and took a big sip from her cup.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Hanging your coat on a hook keeps it off the floor.
story:
Brooklyn put her carrot in her pocket. She and Mom were waiting at the bus stop. "Let's try your coat," said Mom. Brooklyn had dropped her coat on the floor yesterday. It slid under the chair. She could not find it. Today, Mom had hung it on the hook by the door. "Your coat was right there," said Mom. Brooklyn picked it off the hook. The hook had kept it off the floor. It was not dusty. It was not lost.

"Now the zipper," said Mom. Brooklyn pulled the coat on. One arm. Two arms. She held the zipper low. She pulled it up. It stuck. She tried again. Up, up, up it went. "I did it!" said Brooklyn. A furry dog walked by. "I dream of dogs," said Brooklyn. The bus came. "Zip, zip," said Brooklyn, and she climbed on.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much.
story:
Audrey had a cough. It came out in big bounces. "Time to call the pharmacy," said Dad. He picked up the phone. He called Mr. Blue at the corner store. "Your medicine is ready," said Mr. Blue.

At the pharmacy, Audrey saw a yellow sign. The floor was slippery from a wet mop. She held Dad's hand and walked slow. Mr. Blue had a small bag. He had a triangle of white paper taped on it. It said Audrey. Dad paid for the medicine.

At home, Dad gave Audrey a spoon of medicine. She swallowed it down. Later, Mom made warm soup. Audrey took two bites. Then she pushed the bowl away. "I can't eat more," she said. "That is okay," said Mom. "When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much." Audrey yawned. Her blanket was soft. Her cough was small now. "Good night, soup," she said.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: When a birthday cake has candles, a grown-up is the one who lights them.
story:
Mia turned four today. The party was at the big park. Grandma brought a cake with four candles. Mia wanted to light them all by herself.

She grabbed the little matchbox. Dad took it gently. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," he said. "You get to make the wish." Mia pouted a bit. Then Dad lit the candles one by one. The sky was cloudy, so the flames looked extra bright.

Mia took a big breath. She blew and blew. All four candles went out. Everyone clapped. "Happy birthday, Mia!" said her friend Sam. Grandma cut the cake with a safe knife and gave Sam the first big slice, because Sam had skipped his nap and looked sleepy.

Mia handed out plates to everyone. She even saved a seat for Grandpa. Then she licked frosting off her thumb and said, "Next year, can I watch Dad light them again?" Dad laughed. "Yes," he said. "Every year."

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
story:
Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse smiled at him. "Do you know how to wash your hands?" she asked. "With soap?" said Dylan. "Yes! With soap, for twenty seconds. That is a slow count to twenty."

The nurse took Dylan to the little sink. She put soap on his hands. "Can you count to twenty?" she asked. "I can try," said Dylan. They rubbed and counted together. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. The bubbles went down the drain. Dylan's hands were clean and shiny. "Now the germs are off," said the nurse. "We wash our hands after the toilet too."

Then the nurse gave Dylan a snack. A cracker, and a little cup of apple juice. Dylan looked at his hands. He looked at the cracker. He jumped up. "Wait!" he said. He ran to the sink. He put on soap. He counted to twenty all by himself. "Twenty!" he shouted. His hands were clean.

Dylan ran back and took the cracker. "I washed first!" he said. The nurse clapped. Dylan munched his cracker and smiled. He looked out the window at the whole wide world. Then he took a big sip of juice.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
It was a rainy day, so Asher went to the store with his mom. The store had a big wall of crayons. Asher wanted a blue crayon for his rain picture.

A girl named Mia stood there too. She held a dark blue crayon. "That is not blue," said a boy next to her. "It is too dark." Asher felt worried. Maybe there was only one true blue.

Mia put the crayons on the floor. "Let's line them up," she said. Asher helped. First came a light blue, like the sky. Then a middle blue. Then a dark blue, like the night. "They are all still called blue," said Mia. Asher smiled.

He picked two blues, a light one and a dark one. Mom paid for them at the desk. At home, Asher drew rainy clouds. "Light blue for morning," he said. "Dark blue for bedtime."

"Two blues," said Mom. "One box, both true."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Romy sat on the playroom rug. She wanted her red ball. It was on the top shelf, way up high.

Her teddy was on the floor. He was down low. Romy reached up for the ball. It was too far. She reached down for teddy. That was easy.

Then Romy saw a small step stool. She carried it over. She climbed up, up, up. Now she was tall. She grabbed the red ball. "Yes!" she said.

But the ball rolled fast across the rug. Teddy sat there, and the ball bumped him. Ted fell over. Romy climbed down, down, down. She ran slow and careful to teddy.

"Oops, teddy," she said. "Are you mad?" She gave teddy a big hug. Then she gave him the ball too.

Papa came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it's hot," he said. He set it far from teddy. "I will teach you the clean-up song," he said.

Romy looked at the stool. Up the stool, then down. Down, then up. "Papa, up and down are opposites!" she said.

Papa laughed. "Look at that," he said. Then Romy pushed teddy fast, fast, fast in the little wagon.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Library books are shared with many other people, so we take care not to tear or write in them.
story:
Naomi stood in the reading corner. She held her new library card with both hands. It had her name on it in red letters. Today she could pick one book to take home.

She found a big book about stars. Inside was a blank white page at the back. Naomi took out her crayon. She wanted to draw a big yellow circle on that page.

The librarian knelt down beside her. She said, "That book is shared with many other people. We take care not to tear it or write in it."

Naomi looked at the page. Then she looked at the little boy reading on the mat. He would read this book next week. And a girl would read it after him. The book belonged to them too.

Naomi put her crayon away. She asked the librarian for a piece of paper. She drew her big yellow circle on the paper instead. Then she put the paper inside her coat, safe and flat.

The librarian smiled. "Would you like to borrow the star book?" Naomi nodded. She held the book with clean hands and carried it to the desk. "My first book," she said. The librarian stamped it gently. "Two weeks," she said. Naomi hugged the book all the way home.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Layla wanted to find the cookie jar. Grandma said the cookies were a gift for her hands to find.

Layla used her eyes to look. She saw the big red jar. It sat on a shelf. The shelf looked too high. Layla touched the jar with her fingers. It felt smooth and heavy.

Then Layla heard a sound. Pop! The lid came off. A smell came out. She sniffed with her nose. Two little openings took in the yummy smell. "Grandma, my nose has two holes!"

"They are called nostrils," said Grandma. Layla ran to the mirror. She counted the openings in her nose. One, two. Yes, two nostrils!

Layla took a small bite. Her tongue tasted cinnamon. She jumped up and down. "The cookies are found!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house. "Grandma now?" she asked. Daddy shook his head. "Not now, Paisley. Grandma is later. First we drive, then we get there."

Paisley looked out the window. A cow stood in a wild, grassy field. "Cow now!" she said. The cow went behind a hill. "Cow gone now," she said. Daddy laughed. "That's right. Now means right this minute."

Paisley thought about that. Yesterday she had painted an egg at Grandma's house. It was yellow. Today she wanted to paint a blue egg. Tomorrow she would show it to her friend Sam.

"Snack now?" Paisley asked. Her tummy made a little growl. Daddy reached back and gave her a banana. "Now you can eat," he said. Paisley ate it all up.

Soon a red roof came into view. "Grandma's house now!" she said. Grandma waved from the door. Paisley ran to her. "We can paint now?" she asked. Grandma held up her hand. In it was a small white egg, all ready. "Yes, Paisley. Right now."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: A game has rules that all the players follow.
story:
Audrey sat on the soft red rug. Her friends Ben and Mia sat close by. Dad was near the door, folding socks.

"We play the button game," said Mia. She put out three cups. "The button hides under one cup. We take turns. We guess slow, one at a time."

Audrey went first. She pointed to the red cup. No button. Ben went next. He pointed to the blue cup. No button. Then Mia guessed the green cup. The button was there!

"Winners get the button," said Mia.

Then Ben picked up the cups. "Now I move them fast," he said. "And I guess every turn. New rules!"

Audrey stopped playing. Mia stopped too. "That is not the game," she said. Her voice was small and sad. Ben moved the cups alone. Nobody guessed. Nobody laughed.

Audrey tapped his arm. "We all follow the rules," she said. "That is how the game works."

Ben put the cups down. He was quiet. Then he smiled. "Okay. Real rules. One turn each."

They played again. Red cup, blue cup, green cup. Audrey guessed slow and careful. The button was under the red cup!

Dad brought three cups of water. "Careful," he said. "Don't spill."

Audrey held her cup with two hands. She did not spill. She took a slow sip.

"My turn, my turn," said Ben.

Audrey passed the cups around. One for Ben. One for Mia. One for her.

"I win this time!" said Audrey. She held up the button.

"My name goes on the winner list," said Mia, giggling.

"What list?" said Ben.

"The one we make up next!" said Mia.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: While you wait for a turn, you can play with something else.
story:
Charlie was at soccer practice. There was one big red ball. Charlie wanted it right away.

Tommy had the ball first. He kicked it to his friend Ben. Charlie reached out and grabbed it. Tommy said, "Hey! My turn!" The coach blew her whistle. She held up one finger. "One ball, many friends," she said. Then she gave Charlie a small friendly star sticker for his shirt.

The coach pointed to the cones. "Send the little ball over there while you wait," she said. Charlie picked up a little blue ball. He sent it to the wall. It bounced back! He sent it again. Bounce, bounce. That was funny.

Then Tommy ran over. "My turn is done," he said. "Here, Charlie." Charlie got the big red ball at last. He kicked it far. "Nice kick!" said Tommy. Charlie smiled and sent the star sticker a little pat with his hand. "Your turn next," he said to Tommy.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a small scratchy sound, like a tiny animal at the door. She was hungry now. "Is dinner soon?" she asked. Mom said, "Yes. Soon means in a little while." Iris waited. She counted the spoons on the table. One spoon, two spoons, three spoons. Yesterday she had pasta. Today she would have soup. Tomorrow she would have pasta again.

"One, two, three," said Iris. Mom set down the bowls. "Now we eat," said Mom. The soup was warm and yummy. Iris ate it all up. She was not mad anymore. Her tummy was happy.

"After dinner we will have a treat," said Mom. "Later," said Iris. "Yes, later," said Mom. Iris licked her spoon and smiled. "One, two, three spoons of soup for me."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: It is polite to wait until someone finishes talking before you start to speak.
story:
Milo had big news. His tooth was wiggly. He ran to the kitchen. Mom was on the phone. "Mom! Mom! My tooth!" he said. Mom held up one finger. She was still talking. Milo waited. He wiggled his toe instead.

The phone went quiet. Mom smiled at him. "Yes, Milo? What is it?" she asked. "My tooth wiggles!" said Milo. "May I show Dad?" "Of course," said Mom. "Thank you for waiting, Milo."

At dinner, Dad was telling about his shiny new mug. Milo opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He took a bite and waited. Dad stopped talking. There was a quiet moment. "Now, Milo," said Dad. "My tooth wiggles!" said Milo. Dad looked at it. "Wow," he said. Milo grinned. Later, Mom tucked him into bed. The dog came to lick his hand. "Sorry, dog," said Milo. "You cannot sleep here." He closed his eyes. "Good night, tooth."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
James sat at the little table. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. He would paint her favorite flower. But the flower in the book was pink. James had red, blue, yellow and green paint. He had white paint too. But there was no pink.

James looked and looked. He painted a green stem. He painted a green leaf. He stirred his brush in the water and waited. The teacher, Miss Ada, smiled at him. "Take your time," she said. James tapped the table. He tapped his chin. Then he dipped his brush in the red paint. He put a big red dot on his tray.

Next he dipped his brush in the white paint. He stirred it into the red dot. Round and round went the brush. Slowly, the red dot turned pink! James gasped. "It turned pink!" he said. He painted the pink flower on the card. It looked just like the one in the book.

Then James had a small surprise. A drop of pink paint fell off his brush. It landed on the blue paint. Miss Ada laughed. "Now you have a purple spot," she said. James laughed too. He painted the purple spot next to his flower. Grandma would love it.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Pouring slowly helps keep milk from splashing out of the cup.
story:
Lily stood on a little stool in the restaurant kitchen. The cook, Ben, gave her warm toast. "Can I be your helper?" Lily asked. "Yes," said Ben. "Let's make breakfast for Dad."

Lily took the butter knife. She spread the butter, slow and smooth. The butter got soft and shiny on the toast. "Good job," said Ben. "Now the milk."

Lily picked up the big jug. She poured fast. Milk splashed out onto the table! "Oh no," said Lily. Ben wiped the table with a cloth. "Try again," he said. "Pour slowly this time."

Lily tipped the cup high, but she poured slowly, slowly. The milk went up, up, up. It stayed in the cup. No splash. No spill.

"Look, Dad!" said Lily. She set the cup on the tray next to the toast. Dad smiled big. "Milk and toast, my favorite." Lily looked at the clean table. "More milk, Ben? I can pour."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A new pet may hide at first while it gets used to its new home.
story:
Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish. She saw birds. Then she saw a small gray kitten. "I want that one," said Ella. Dad said, "Okay. We will need food and a warm blanket too." Dad carried the big bag of food. It was heavy and strong. Ella carried the little blanket.

At home, Ella opened the cage. The kitten ran fast. It went under Ella's bed. It did not come out. Ella looked and looked. "Where did it go?" she said. The phone did ring, but Ella stayed very still. She sat on the floor by the bed. She waited. She waited more.

Then one little paw came out. Then the whole kitten came out. Ella sat very still. The kitten walked to her. It sniffed her hand. It rubbed her arm. "Hello," said Ella softly. The kitten sat in her lap.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together.
story:
Ayla stood in the band room. Her drum sat on the floor. Ben had a drum too.

"Can we play together?" Ayla asked.

"Yes," said Ben. "Let's try."

They played. Ayla went fast. Ben went fast too. Then faster. Then fastest. The sound got all mixed up. They stopped.

"Why did it sound funny?" Ayla asked.

"Maybe we went too fast," said Ben.

Miss Kay came over. She tapped her drum one, two, three, four. Slow and steady. "Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together," she said.

Ayla listened. Then she tapped one, two, three, four. Ben tapped too. Same speed.

"Now let's play," said Ayla.

They played. Slow and steady. Together.

"Shop for drums with me next time," said Ben. Ayla smiled and zipped her jacket straight up. Then she tapped the beat one more time, just for fun.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Other languages have their own words for thank you, like 'gracias' in Spanish.
story:
Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was empty. She wanted more rice.

"Please may I have more rice?" she asked. Daddy smiled. He gave her a big spoonful. "Thank you," said Sienna.

Then she reached for the milk. Oops. The cup tipped over. Milk ran across the table. "Sorry," said Sienna. Daddy wiped it up. "Can you help me, please?" he asked. Sienna ran to get a towel. She wiped and wiped. One, two, three swipes. The table was dry again.

Then a knock came at the door. It was Mateo, her new friend from the playground. He sat down at the table too. Mama gave him some rice. "Gracias," said Mateo.

Sienna blinked. What did that mean? "Gracias means thank you," said Mateo. "We say it in Spanish."

Sienna tried the new word. "Grah-see-as," she said slowly. Mateo laughed and clapped. She tried again. "Gracias!" This time it slid out just right.

Mama put a cookie on Sienna's plate. Sienna looked at Mateo. "Gracias, Mama," she said.

Mateo held out his hand for a high five. "Gracias to you too," he said.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or helps us.
story:
Camille sat down at the dinner table. Grandma put a big bowl of peas in front of her. "These are for you," Grandma said. Camille grabbed the spoon and started eating right away.

"Can I have some peas too?" asked her brother Leo. Camille looked at the bowl. She pushed it across the table to him. Leo put some peas on his plate. Then he pushed the bowl back. "Your turn," he said. Camille took some more. Back and forth the bowl went. Camille giggled. Sharing made the bowl go around like a ride.

Dad used a knife to cut the bread. "One piece for you, one for Leo," he said. Two pieces, both the same size. Camille looked at them. The same! That felt good.

After dinner, Grandma held out a small box. Inside was a shiny red hair clip. Camille put it in her hair. She ran to the mirror. Then she thought of Grandma standing there. She ran back and gave Grandma a hug. "Thank you," she said. Grandma smiled big. "Thank you back," said Grandma. "And now I thank you for this hug."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Jaxson followed Mom into the kitchen. They had shopped for apples, and his tummy was hungry. Mom put a pot on the stove. "The stove is hot," Mom said. She turned the knob. Jaxson stayed back and watched. The pot went sizzle, sizzle. Mom stirred the apples with a big spoon.

Then Jaxson saw something on the wall. It was a little box with holes. He wanted to poke it with his spoon. "Mom, what is this?" he asked. Mom came right over. "That is an outlet," she said. "We never put fingers or spoons in outlets." Mom gave him a job instead. "Put the napkins on the table," she said.

Jaxson carried the napkins one by one. He set them down just right. Then he sat on his chair and waited. Soon Mom brought warm apple sauce. Jaxson took a big bite. "Yum," he said, and licked his spoon.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Tomorrow is the day after today.
story:
Bennett stood by his bedroom window. He was looking for the red swing at Leo's house. "Can I go on the swing now?" he asked. Mom shook her head. "Not now, sweet pea. You will go tomorrow."

Bennett frowned. "What is tomorrow?" Mom pointed at the sky. "First the sun will sleep. Then you will sleep too. Then it will be tomorrow, and you will go to Leo."

Bennett did not want to sleep. He wanted the swing now. So he waited. He watched the sky. The sun went down, down, down. The sky turned dark. The streetlights came on, round like little moons.

"Now is it tomorrow?" Bennett asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "You have to sleep first. Tomorrow comes after sleeping."

Bennett got into his little bed. He hugged his soft bear. "Sleep now, swing tomorrow," he said. "Sleep now, swing tomorrow." He closed his eyes. His dreams went round and round, all the way to Leo's red swing.

When Bennett woke up, the sun was bright. "Mom! Is it tomorrow?" Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is tomorrow now." Bennett ran to the window. There was the swing, waiting in the sun. "I did not miss it," he said.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
story:
Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was so thirsty. "Milk, please!" she said. Dad gave her a cup, and she drank it all up.

Then Mom brought in the laundry basket. "Can you help sort?" Mom asked. Rosalie jumped up. She held up a sock. "A sock!" she laughed. She put it with the teddy bear and the toy truck.

Mom shook her head, smiling. "No, no. Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes." Rosalie gasped. She looked at the shirt in her hand. She looked at the hat. She put them all in one pile, quick quick quick. Then she put the teddy bear with the toys.

"Look, Mom! Clothes here! Toys there!" The pile was big. Dad clapped loud. "What a good helper. That calls for a gift." He slid a warm cookie onto her plate. It smelled sweet. Rosalie took a big bite. "Yum!" she said.
